newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Chidambaram wants lower interest rates.
newsitem.headline: India's Chidambaram wants lower interest rates.

text.p: Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram said on Saturday that he would like to see interest rates decline and will press the central bank to ensure adequate credit flows to industry.

Chidambaram told Reuters in an interview that real interest rates are lower now than they were when Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's centre-left government took office last June, but that industry felt they were high.
"As a principle I would like interest rates to soften," he said. "I think industry will be competitive, or to be more accurate, more competitive if interest rates are lower."

The finance minister said interest rates, adjusted for inflation, were currently at about eight or nine percent, down from 17-18 percent last June. But he said Japanese interest rates were even lower, giving industry there an advantage.

Chidambaram said he would discuss the possibility of lower interest rates when he meets Reserve Bank of India (RBI) officials in the capital on Monday for a crucial meeting being closely watched by financial markets and industry.
"Yes, I've said so, that one of the things we will discuss is interest rates, and the possibility of interest rates coming down a bit," he said.
Chidambaram said Monday's meeting would provide an opportunity to discuss a new credit policy that the RBI is set to announce next month.

"We also need to discuss the need to maintain price stability. I said in my budget speech that maintaining price stability is very high on the government's agenda. We also need to discuss the surge in foreign exchange inflows," he said.

The RBI has recently had to buy dollars to prevent the rupee from appreciating. The finance minister said large inflows of dollars made foreign exchange reserves appear healthy but could also fuel inflation.

Chidambaram said he and the RBI would also discuss flows of bank credit to industry. "There is still some feeling in the market that adequate credit is not flowing for productive purposes, that interest rates are still high," he said.
"Given the mood in industry today, it is necessary to ensure that adequate credit is made available to industry, to agriculture for productive purposes," he said.
Chidambaram said the foreign exchange market must determine the value of the rupee against the U.S. dollar.

Asked if there was room for the rupee to depreciate against the U.S. dollar, he said: "We don't talk of depreciating the rupee or devaluing the rupee. As I have said, it is the market which must determine the level of the rupee."
On Friday the rupee closed at 35.865/870 against the dollar.
Chidambaram said he shared the RBI's concern that there should not be volatility in the rupee exchange rate.
Asked if India could prevent recent large inflows of dollars from stoking inflation by relaxing controls on imports of consumer goods, he said: "I have said it is an option."
Chidambaram said he was confident the government would meet its tax revenue target for 1997/98 (April-March) despite interest rate cuts which he proposed in the government's budget last month.
The finance minister also predicted parliament would adopt the budget, which slashed corporate and income tax rates, while projecting less red ink.
"I think what will eventually prevail is the overall public perception of the budget," he said. "I believe the budget will pass."
